title: Present and imperfect subjunctive

objectives.can: Recognise present and imperfect subjunctives and parse them.
Read a subjunctive in a main clause as a wish, an exhortation, a command or a doubt.

explanation.summary: The indicative states facts. The subjunctive is another mood, used for what is wished, urged, feared, aimed at or merely imagined. It has its own endings, and it is common in the Vulgate: the Lord's Prayer is largely made of subjunctives. This lesson teaches how to recognise the present and imperfect subjunctive, and how to read it when it stands alone in a main clause.

sections.heading: What the subjunctive is
body: Mood is the speaker's attitude to what is said. Indicative: it happens. Imperative: do it. Subjunctive: let it happen, may it happen, should it happen, so that it may happen. English has few subjunctive forms ('God save the king', 'if I were you'), so there is no single English equivalent for the Latin subjunctive. Its meaning comes from the clause it stands in, and translators change it freely.

The Latin subjunctive has four tenses (present, imperfect, perfect, pluperfect), each with active and passive. This lesson covers the first two. The tense of a subjunctive is less about time than about its place in a sequence, a point taken up later; for now the forms are what matter.

sections.heading: The present subjunctive
body: The present subjunctive is made from the present stem by changing the vowel before the personal ending. In the first conjugation the stem vowel a becomes e: *laudat* (indicative) gives *laudet* (subjunctive). In the other conjugations an a is put in: *timet* gives *timeat*, *regit* gives *regat*, *audit* gives *audiat*, and *facit* gives *faciat*. The personal endings are those of the present: -m, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt (-r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -mini, -ntur in the passive).

The verb *sum* has its own forms: *sim*, *sis*, *sit*, *simus*, *sitis*, *sint*. Others are irregular too: *fio* has *fiat*, *do* has *det* and *dem*, *volo* has *velit*. Learn the common ones by heart; *fiat* in particular is everywhere.
A useful rule: if a first-conjugation word has -e- where you expect -a-, or a verb of another conjugation has -a- where you expect -e- or -i-, you have a present subjunctive.

sections.heading: The imperfect subjunctive
body: The imperfect subjunctive is the easiest tense to recognise. Take the present infinitive and add the personal endings: *habere* gives *haberet*, *ascendere* gives *ascenderet*, *audire* gives *audiret*. For *sum* the infinitive is *esse*, so the forms are *essem*, *esses*, *esset*, *essemus*, *essetis*, *essent*. Wherever you see -ret, -rent, -res or -remus after a vowel, suspect it.

The passive and the deponent verbs add the passive endings to the same infinitive-like base: *impleretur*, *nasceretur*, *loquerentur*. The imperfect subjunctive always shows the -re- of the infinitive before the personal ending, which keeps it apart from the future indicative.

sections.heading: The subjunctive in a main clause
body: Most subjunctives in Latin stand in subordinate clauses and are explained in later lessons (*ut daret*, *ut pereat*). Four uses occur in the main clause, all with the present subjunctive and all common in prayer.

A wish or hope: *fiat lux*, 'let there be light'; *sanctificetur nomen tuum*, 'may your name be made holy'; *adveniat regnum tuum*, 'may your kingdom come'. An exhortation to oneself and others, with the first person plural: *adoremus*, 'let us worship'; *non scindamus eam*, 'let us not tear it'. A prohibition, with *ne* and the second person: *ne timeas*, 'do not fear'; *ne inducas*, 'do not lead'. A doubt or deliberative question, in the first person: *quid faciam?*, 'what am I to do?'. The usual negative with all of these is *ne*; the Vulgate sometimes uses *non* instead, as in *non scindamus eam*.

The third person with a wish is often called the optative or jussive; the first plural, hortatory. You need not memorise the labels, but you should recognise the meaning: when a main-clause verb is a present subjunctive, the sentence is a wish, an urging, a command or a question about what to do, not a statement.

misunderstandings: A subjunctive is not a tense of the indicative. *timeat* is not 'he will fear' and not 'he was fearing'; it is another mood altogether.

The imperfect subjunctive does not mean 'was doing'. *haberet* is made from the infinitive and is used mostly in subordinate clauses; depending on the clause it may be translated with a plain past, with 'would' or with 'might'.

The first person singular present subjunctive of the 3rd and 4th conjugations (*audiam*, *faciam*) looks exactly like the future indicative. The sentence decides: *quid faciam?* may be read as either 'what shall I do?' or 'what am I to do?'.
Not every -ret is a subjunctive in a main clause. The imperfect subjunctive usually stands in a subordinate clause, with *ut*, *cum* or *si*. Look for the conjunction first.

deeper.heading: Why 'let there be'?
body: Latin grammarians note that *fiat* has no exact English match. The old English subjunctive 'be it so' is the nearest, which is why the Latin liturgy's *fiat* is borrowed unchanged. Its force is wish-like when said of something that depends on God, command-like when said of something that depends on a person.

examples.analysis: *inducas* is the present subjunctive of *induco*, second person singular, with *ne*: a prohibition, 'do not lead'. The vowel has changed from -is (indicative) to -as. Latin uses *ne* with the present subjunctive for a polite or prayerful prohibition.

examples.analysis: *adoremus*, *procidamus* and *ploremus* are first person plural present subjunctives: 'let us worship, let us fall down, let us weep'. The -emus ending of the first conjugation, and -amus after a 3rd-conjugation stem, mark the exhortation.

examples.analysis: *ascenderet* and *sederet* are imperfect subjunctives of *ascendo* and *sedeo*, third person singular. Each is the infinitive (*ascendere*, *sedere*) plus -t. They stand in the clause after *ut*, 'asked Philip that he come up and sit'. This is a subordinate clause, to be taken up in a later lesson; here, learn to see the form.
